Solve the equation below. \[7=5 x-8\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[7=5 x-8\] Add 8 to both sides of the equation.

\[15=5 x\]

Divide both sides of the equation by 5.

\[3=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=3\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 3 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[7\stackrel{?}{=}5 (3)-8\]

\[7 \stackrel{?}{=} 15-8\]

\[7 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 7\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=3\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[23=7 x+9\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[23=7 x+9\] Subtract 9 from both sides of the equation.

\[14=7 x\]

Divide both sides of the equation by 7.

\[2=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=2\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 2 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[23\stackrel{?}{=}7 (2)+9\]

\[23 \stackrel{?}{=} 14+9\]

\[23 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 23\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=2\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[2=\frac{x-3}{4}\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[2=\frac{x-3}{4}\] Multiply both sides of the equation by 4.

\[8=x-3\]

Add 3 to both sides of the equation.

\[11=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=11\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 11 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[2\stackrel{?}{=}\frac{(11)-3}{4}\]

\[2 \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{8}{4}\]

\[2 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 2\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=11\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[2=\frac{x}{3}-2\]

Rewrite the given equation. \[2=\frac{x}{3}-2\] Add 2 to both sides of the equation.

\[4=\frac{x}{3}\]

Multiply both sides of the equation by 3.

\[12=x\]

Switch sides (which is allowed because equality is commutative).

\[x=12\]

You can check your possible answer by substituting 12 for \(x\) in the original equation.

\[2\stackrel{?}{=}\frac{(12)}{3}-2\]

\[2 \stackrel{?}{=} 4-2\]

\[2 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 2\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=12\) is a solution to the equation.

So, indeed we see that \(x=7\) is a solution to the equation.

Solve the equation below. \[2=\frac{x+3}{5}\]

\[2 \stackrel{\checkmark}{=} 2\]

So, indeed we see that \(x=7\) is a solution to the equation.

Consider the shifted square-root function graphed below:


Which equation represents the plotted curve?

The parent function, \(y=\sqrt{x}\), has been shifted \(5\) units left and \(4\) units down.

The correct answer is \[y=\sqrt{x+5}-4\]

Notice the horizontal translation is counterintuitive. The horizontal coordinate transformation is the INVERSE of the argument expression, whereas the vertical coordinate transformation is simply the outer operations.

\[(a,b)~\to~(a-5,b-4)\]

where \((a,b)\) is a solution to the parent equation \(\sqrt{a}=b\). For example, \(\sqrt{0}=0\) or \(\sqrt{1}=1\) or \(\sqrt{4}=2\) or \(\sqrt{9}=3\)... Thus from curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to curve \(y=\sqrt{x+5}-4\), we have the following coordinate transformations:

\[(0,0) \to (-5,-4)\] \[(1,1) \to (-4,-3)\] \[(4,2) \to (-1,-2)\] \[(9,3) \to (4,-1)\]

Consider the shifted square-root function graphed below:


Which equation represents the plotted curve?

The parent function, \(y=\sqrt{x}\), has been shifted \(5\) units right and \(3\) units down.

The correct answer is \[y=\sqrt{x-5}-3\]

Notice the horizontal translation is counterintuitive. The horizontal coordinate transformation is the INVERSE of the argument expression, whereas the vertical coordinate transformation is simply the outer operations.

\[(a,b)~\to~(a+5,b-3)\]

where \((a,b)\) is a solution to the parent equation \(\sqrt{a}=b\). For example, \(\sqrt{0}=0\) or \(\sqrt{1}=1\) or \(\sqrt{4}=2\) or \(\sqrt{9}=3\)... Thus from curve \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to curve \(y=\sqrt{x-5}-3\), we have the following coordinate transformations:

\[(0,0) \to (5,-3)\] \[(1,1) \to (6,-2)\] \[(4,2) \to (9,-1)\] \[(9,3) \to (14,0)\]

Calculate the discriminant of the following quadratic function:

\[y~=~{2}x^{2}+{5}x+{14}\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=2\] \[b=5\] \[c=14\]

Use the formula for the disciminant.

\[D=(5)^2-4(2)(14)\]

\[D=-87\]

The discriminant, \(D=-87\), is negative, so there are no \(x\)-intercepts.

Calculate the discriminant of the following quadratic function:

\[y~=~{-12}x^{2}-{12}x-{3}\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=-12\] \[b=-12\] \[c=-3\]

Use the formula for the disciminant.

\[D=(-12)^2-4(-12)(-3)\]

\[D=0\]

The discriminant, \(D=0\), is zero, so there is one \(x\)-intercept.

Calculate the discriminant of the following quadratic function:

\[y~=~{12}x^{2}-{16}x+{10}\]

Identify the coefficients.

\[a=12\] \[b=-16\] \[c=10\]

Use the formula for the disciminant.

\[D=(-16)^2-4(12)(10)\]

\[D=-224\]

The discriminant, \(D=-224\), is negative, so there are no \(x\)-intercepts.

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x-{5})^2~=~16\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-4\) and \(4\) produce \(16\).

\[(x-{5})^2~=~16\]

\[x-{5}~=~\pm4\]

\[x~=~5\pm4\]

So the two solutions are \(x=9\) and \(x=1\).

Simplify the following powers of \(i\).

  • \(i^{55}=\)
  • \(i^{56}=\)
  • \(i^{69}=\)
  • \(i^{74}=\)
  • \(i^{78}=\)

For any positive integer \(n\), we can evaluate \(i^n\) by determining the remainder when \(n\) is divided by 4.

Remainder of \(n/4\) \(i^n\)
0 \(1\)
1 \(i\)
2 \(-1\)
3 \(-i\)

In computer programming, the modulo operator returns the remainder. This operation is used so frequently, that it is often abbreviated to a single symbol (for example, in Python, 5%2 represents the remainder when 5 is divided by 2.)

I will represent the remainders using the Desmos notation.

  • \(\mathrm{mod}(55,4)=3\) so \(i^{55}=-i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(56,4)=0\) so \(i^{56}=1\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(69,4)=1\) so \(i^{69}=i\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(74,4)=2\) so \(i^{74}=-1\)
  • \(\mathrm{mod}(78,4)=2\) so \(i^{78}=-1\)

To find the remainder using a scientific calculator, I would divide by 4, floor the result, multiply by 4, and subtract that amount from the original.

\[\mathrm{mod}(x,4)~=~x-4\cdot \left\lfloor\frac{x}{4}\right\rfloor\]

Let \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) be two complex numbers. \[z_1 = -4-8i\] \[z_2 = 8-3i\] Find the product. \[z_1 \cdot z_2 = ~?\]

Type your answer precisely, with no spaces, using digits, "-", "+", and "i". If the real term is nonzero, put it first. If either component is zero, do not include that term. If both components are zero, type "0" without the quotes. Instead of writing "1i" or "-1i" just write "i" or "-i".

To multiply complex numbers, follow a procedure similar to FOIL, but remember \(i^2=-1\).

\[(-4-8i)(8-3i)\]

\[\Big((-4)+(-8i)\Big)\Big((8)+(-3i)\Big)\]

\[(-4)(8)~~+~~(-4)(-3i)~~+~~(-8i)(8)~~+~~(-8i)(-3i)\] \[-32~~+~~(12)i~~+~~(-64)i ~~+~~(24)i^2\]

You could also use a box to multiply.

* \(-4\) \(-8i\)
\(8\) \(-32\) \(-64i\)
\(-3i\) \(12i\) \(24i^2\)

\[-32~~+~~(12)i~~+~~(-64)i ~~+~~(24)i^2\]

Remember that \(i^2=-1\).

\[-32~~+~~(12)i~~+~~(-64)i~~+~~(-24)\]

Let's group similar terms. We put the real terms to the left and the imaginary terms to the right.

\[-32~~+~~(-24)~~+~~(12)i~~+~~(-64)i\] Combine the real terms and combine the imaginary terms.

\[-56-52i\]

Find all solutions to the equation below:

\[(x+{6})^2~=~49\]

Notice, because the squaring function is NOT one-to-one, when we "undo" it on both sides of an equation, we need to consider multiple possibilities.

In this case, you should know that, when squared, both \(-7\) and \(7\) produce \(49\).

\[(x+{6})^2~=~49\]

\[x+{6}~=~\pm7\]

\[x~=~-6\pm7\]

So the two solutions are \(x=1\) and \(x=-13\).

Solve the equation:

\[\sqrt{14x-56}+4=2x-3\]

\[\sqrt{14x-56}+4=2x-3\]

Subtract 4 from both sides.

\[\sqrt{14x-56}=2x-7\]

Square both sides.\[14x-56=(2x-7)^2\]

Expand the right side.\[14x-56=4x^2-28x+49\]

Subtract \(14x-56\) from both sides.\[0=4x^2-42x+105\]

Use the quadratic formula.

\[x=\frac{-(-42)\pm\sqrt{(-42)^2-4(4)(105)}}{2(4)}\]

Simplify.\[x=\frac{42\pm\sqrt{1764-1680}}{8}\]

Simplify.\[x=\frac{42\pm\sqrt{84}}{8}\]

Simplify the radical.\[x=\frac{42\pm2\sqrt{21}}{8}\]

Simplify based on common factor of 2.

\[x=\frac{21\pm\sqrt{21}}{4}\]

Simplify.\[x=\frac{29\pm\sqrt{9}}{8}\]

Simplify the radical.\[x=\frac{29\pm3}{8}\]

Let function \(f\) represent a cubic polynomial. One solution to the equation \(f(x)=0\) is \(x=\frac{9}{8}\). Which of the following is a known factor of \(f\)?

Solutions to \(f(x)=0\) correspond to the factors of \(f\) equaling zero. So, if a factor of \(f\) is \(ax+b\), then we know \(ax+b=0\), which if we solve for \(x\) gives us \(x=\frac{-b}{a}\).

If we take this logic backwards, a solution of \(x=\frac{c}{d}\) implies \(dx-c\) is a factor. In this case, we were told the solution is:

\[x=\frac{9}{8}\]

Which implies that the linear binomial \(8x-9\) is a factor. We can check that this factor gives that solution by solving \(8x-9=0\).

Solutions to \(f(x)=0\) correspond to the factors of \(f\) equaling zero. So, if a factor of \(f\) is \(ax+b\), then we know \(ax+b=0\), which if we solve for \(x\) gives us \(x=\frac{-b}{a}\).

If we take this logic backwards, a solution of \(x=\frac{c}{d}\) implies \(dx-c\) is a factor. In this case, we were told the solution is:

\[x=\frac{7}{4}\]

Which implies that the linear binomial \(4x-7\) is a factor. We can check that this factor gives that solution by solving \(4x-7=0\).
